level.w1-l3.mission: Get the ball into the valley in 15 steps or fewer. Before each step, choose how far to go.
level.w1-l3.hint1: Watch the hollow ball before you step: it shows where you will land. Is it closer to the valley, or past it?
level.w1-l3.hint2: The arrow always points downhill. Where the ground is steep, a big step overshoots; where it is flat, a small step wastes moves.
level.w1-l3.hint3: Start small, around 0.08, while the slope is steep. Once the ball is in the long valley, raise the step size to about 0.28.
level.w1-l3.debrief: That was gradient descent. Each step moves the model's parameters against the slope of the loss, and your step size is the learning rate. Too small wastes steps, too large overshoots, and the best optimizers adapt the step as the slope changes.
level.w1-l1.mission: These points follow a trend. Drag the two handles so the line runs through the middle of the cloud, then check your line.
level.w1-l1.hint1: The thin vertical lines show how far each point is from your line. Try to make them short everywhere, not just in one place.
level.w1-l1.hint2: A good line has about as many points above it as below it, at both ends of the cloud.
level.w1-l1.hint3: Put the left handle near 6 and the right handle near 18.4, then check.
level.w1-l1.debrief: You just fit a linear model: ŷ = w·x + b. Moving the handles chose the slope w and the intercept b, and the error lines you shrank are the model's mistakes. The third star checked that your line also works on points it never saw.
level.w1-l2.mission: Now every move shows the loss: the average squared error of your line. Make it as low as you can in 20 moves or fewer, then check.
level.w1-l2.hint1: Watch the loss after each move. If it went up, move back the other way.
level.w1-l2.hint2: Errors are squared, so a far-away point counts a lot. Aim through the middle of the whole cloud, not just the nearby points.
level.w1-l2.hint3: Put the left handle near 5.7 and the right handle near 19, then nudge each one until the loss stops dropping.
level.w1-l2.debrief: That number was the loss, here the mean squared error. Training a model means searching for the parameters that make it as small as possible. You searched by hand; in the next levels, gradient descent does the searching for you.
level.w1-l4.mission: This time gradient descent moves the line for you. Choose a learning rate and press Train. The line has to settle on the data within 50 epochs without blowing up.
level.w1-l4.hint1: Try the extremes first: a very small rate, then a very large one. Watch how the loss curve behaves each time.
level.w1-l4.hint2: A curve that falls slowly and smoothly means the rate is too small. A curve that zigzags or climbs means it is too large.
level.w1-l4.hint3: The fastest rates for this data sit between about 0.4 and 0.7.
level.w1-l4.debrief: The learning rate is the size of each gradient-descent step. Too small and training crawls; too large and every step overshoots, until the loss bounces or explodes. In between is a sweet spot that converges in a handful of epochs, and finding it is one of the first things you tune on any real model.
level.w1-l5.mission: This landscape has several valleys, and only one is the deepest. Choose where the ball starts, then roll it. Gradient descent will carry it downhill into whichever valley it starts above.
level.w1-l5.hint1: The ball can only feel the slope right under it. It will stop at the bottom of the first valley it rolls into, deep or not.
level.w1-l5.hint2: Look for the valley with the most rings around it: more rings means deeper. Then find the high ground that drains into it.
level.w1-l5.hint3: The deepest valley is on the right, a little below the middle. Start anywhere on the right third of the map.
level.w1-l5.debrief: The ball stopped in a local minimum whenever it started in the wrong valley: gradient descent only follows the slope under it, so where you start decides where you end up. Real training has the same problem, which is why starting points, randomness and restarts matter.
level.w1-l6.mission: Some of these measurements are broken, and they drag the best-fit line off the trend. Remove the bad points, then check the line against fresh data it has never seen.
level.w1-l6.hint1: Watch the line as you remove a point. A bad point makes the line jump; a normal point barely moves it.
level.w1-l6.hint2: The long error lines point at the suspects: points far from where the rest of the cloud says they should be.
level.w1-l6.hint3: There are four broken points, all at the right end and far below the others.
level.w1-l6.debrief: Those points were outliers: bad measurements far from the pattern. Mean squared error squares every error, so a few far-away points can pull the whole line off. Cleaning them fixed the model on new data, and keeping the good points kept it honest; deleting real data just because it doesn't fit is its own mistake.
level.w1-l7.mission: This model has two features, and one is ten times bigger than the other. Train it at least 3 times faster than the best anyone can manage without scaling.
level.w1-l7.hint1: First press Train as it is. That run is about as fast as it gets without scaling: any bigger learning rate blows up.
level.w1-l7.hint2: The big feature makes the loss valley long and narrow, so the learning rate has to stay tiny. Scaling makes both features the same size, and the valley becomes round.
level.w1-l7.hint3: Turn on scaling, then raise the learning rate to around 0.3 to 0.6.
level.w1-l7.debrief: Feature scaling puts every feature on the same footing: minus its mean, divided by its spread. Unscaled, one big feature forces a tiny learning rate, and training crawls along a long, narrow valley. Scaled, the valley is round, a much larger learning rate is safe, and training converges in a few epochs. Scale your features before gradient descent.
level.w1-l8.mission: Everything from World 1 at once: noisy data with broken points, a feature on a large scale, and a tight budget. Train a line that fits fresh data, converging within 30 epochs.
level.w1-l8.hint1: Three things are wrong here. Press Train once as it is, then read what went wrong.
level.w1-l8.hint2: The large x values make the loss valley so narrow that every learning rate on the slider blows up. And a few points far below the others pull the line down.
level.w1-l8.hint3: Remove the four low points at the right end, turn on scaling, and use a learning rate near 0.5.
level.w1-l8.debrief: That is the everyday recipe for training a model: clean the data, scale the features, then tune the learning rate. Skip any one of them and training blows up, crawls, or learns the wrong thing. World 1, the Valley of Loss, is complete.
level.w2-l1.mission: Two kingdoms share this plain. Drag the two handles to draw a straight border, so each kingdom's people end up on its own side. At least 90% must be on the right side.
level.w2-l1.hint1: The shading shows each kingdom's side. If most people sit in the wrong colour, press Swap sides.
level.w2-l1.hint2: The two groups lean: one sits lower left, the other upper right. A border that follows that lean works best.
level.w2-l1.hint3: Put one handle near the top left corner and the other near the bottom right corner, through the gap between the groups.
level.w2-l1.debrief: You just built a classifier. A straight border, w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0, splits the plane into two classes: that is the decision boundary of a linear model like logistic regression. Notice that the border with the most training points right is not always the one that works best on new points.
level.w2-l2.mission: This model gives each point a probability of being a circle. Move the threshold and the slope until every point gets at least 80% for its own kind, then check. Be confident, but not blindly so.
level.w2-l2.hint1: The threshold is where the curve crosses 50%. Put it in the empty gap between the squares and the circles.
level.w2-l2.hint2: A steeper slope makes the model more certain. Too gentle and nobody reaches 80%; too steep and new points near the border get confidently wrong answers.
level.w2-l2.debrief: That S-shaped curve is the sigmoid: it turns a score into a probability. Logistic regression outputs these probabilities, not just a yes or no. The threshold decides the class; the slope decides how sure it is. A model that is certain about everything pays heavily, in log loss, for every mistake on new data.
level.w2-l3.mission: The circle kingdom sits in the middle, surrounded by the square kingdom. No straight border can split them. Choose which features the model sees, train it, and get at least 95% right.
level.w2-l3.hint1: Train with x₁ and x₂ first. A model that only sees x₁ and x₂ can only ever draw a straight border.
level.w2-l3.hint2: Distance from the centre separates the kingdoms. Which features grow with distance from the centre, whatever the direction?
level.w2-l3.hint3: x₁² + x₂² is the squared distance from the centre. Give the model exactly those two features.
level.w2-l3.debrief: The model is still linear, but in new features. On x₁² and x₂², a straight border becomes a circle on the map. That is feature engineering: reshaping the inputs so a simple model can capture a curved pattern. Adding every feature you can think of fits the training points too, but it starts to slip on new ones.
level.w2-l4.mission: Only twenty people have been surveyed. Choose how flexible the border may be, train to see it, then check it on the rest of the kingdom: it must get at least 85% of new people right.
level.w2-l4.hint1: Train at the highest complexity and look at the border. Does it look like the real divide between two groups, or like it is chasing single points?
level.w2-l4.hint2: With so few points, a flexible model can bend around every one of them, noise included. The training score says nothing about new people.
level.w2-l4.hint3: Complexity 1, a straight border, generalizes best on this data.
level.w2-l4.debrief: That was overfitting: the complex model memorized twenty noisy points, got 100% of them right, and did worse on everyone else. With little data, the simplest model that fits is usually the best. Training accuracy measures memory; only new data measures learning.
level.w2-l5.mission: This model has 27 inputs and loves to memorize: it scores far better on the people it was trained on than on anyone new. Turn up the regularization until both scores agree, within 5 points, while still getting at least 85% of new people right.
level.w2-l5.hint1: Train at 0 and look at the border: it twists around single training points. That is where the gap comes from.
level.w2-l5.hint2: Regularization makes large weights expensive, so the border has to stay smooth. A little goes a long way; too much and the model can't even fit what it has seen.
level.w2-l5.debrief: That was regularization: instead of taking inputs away, you kept all 27 and charged the model for using big weights. The border smoothed out, the training score dropped a little, and the two scores met. Push too hard and the model underfits: now it's wrong about the training points too. The right strength is found by checking on data the model hasn't seen.
level.w2-l6.mission: Only one person in ten comes from the hill clans (the green circles). The census keeps missing them. Train a border that finds at least 80% of the hill folk among new people.
level.w2-l6.hint1: Train at ×1 and count: the model gets almost every lowlander right, and that alone scores about 90%. Missing hill folk costs it almost nothing.
level.w2-l6.hint2: Make each hill-clan point count more, so a miss hurts the model as much as missing many lowlanders.
level.w2-l6.hint3: There are about ten lowlanders for every hill-clan person. Try a weight near ×10.
level.w2-l6.debrief: That was class imbalance: when one class is rare, a model can score high accuracy by mostly ignoring it, so accuracy alone lies. Recall asks the right question: of the people you were meant to find, how many did you find? Copying the rare class (oversampling) or weighting it rebalances the training. Push it too far and you start flagging everyone.
level.w2-l7.mission: The king invites hill-clan elders to council, but every invitation costs a rider. The model is trained; you choose how sure it must be before it sends one. Among new people, invite at least 75% of the hill folk, and make sure at least 65% of invitations reach hill folk.
level.w2-l7.hint1: The matrix shows the training people: hill folk found or missed, lowlanders invited by mistake or rightly left out. Check starts from the default threshold 0.5. Look at the missed hill folk.
level.w2-l7.hint2: Lowering the threshold sends invitations to people the model is less sure about: more hill folk found (recall up), but more lowlanders invited too (precision down).
level.w2-l7.hint3: Aim for both numbers under the matrix to clear their targets with a little room: around 0.25 to 0.35.
level.w2-l7.debrief: You just traded precision for recall. Recall asks: of the people you should find, how many did you? Precision asks: of the people you picked, how many were right? One threshold moves both in opposite directions, and the confusion matrix shows exactly what each choice costs. Which balance is right depends on what a miss and a false alarm cost.
level.w2-l8.mission: Raiders hide among the villages at the heart of the plains: about one person in seven, and the records are noisy. Flag them so the border holds on new people: a hidden F1 score of at least 0.85. Every tool from this world is yours.
level.w2-l8.hint1: A straight border can't enclose the heart of the plains, and flagging nobody scores well on accuracy but F1 0. Start by giving the model a curve.
level.w2-l8.hint2: A curve alone falls just short: raiders are rare, so the model is too shy to flag them. Lower the threshold, or give raider points more weight (then raise the threshold to match).
level.w2-l8.hint3: Degree 2 is enough for a round border; higher degrees chase the noise unless you regularize. Try degree 2, regularization 0.02, threshold 0.3.
level.w2-l8.debrief: You won the Boundary Plains. A curve for the shape, restraint against the noise, a fair say for the rare class, and a threshold chosen for the goal. F1 kept you honest: it is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it only rises when both do. These are the everyday decisions of real classification work.
level.w1-l1.notes.idea: A model is a rule that turns an input into a prediction. The simplest one for numbers is a straight line, ŷ = w·x + b: the slope w says how much the prediction grows when x grows by 1, and the intercept b is where the line starts. Fitting means choosing w and b so the line follows the trend in the data.
level.w1-l1.notes.controls: Drag the two orange handles, or focus one and use the arrow keys (hold Shift for bigger moves). Each handle sets the height of one end of the line, so together they set both the slope and the intercept. Press Check my line when you're happy.
level.w1-l1.notes.reading: The short vertical lines are the errors: how far each point is from your line. A good fit keeps them short everywhere, with points spread evenly above and below along the whole line, not just close at one end.
level.w1-l2.notes.idea: To improve a line you need one number that says how wrong it is: the loss. Here it is the mean squared error. Take each point's error, square it, and average them. Squaring makes big misses count far more than small ones, and a perfect fit would score 0.
level.w1-l2.notes.controls: The same handles as before, but now you have a limited number of moves. The loss updates after every move, so you can tell straight away whether a change helped.
level.w1-l2.notes.reading: Watch the loss and your best so far. If a move made the loss go up, move back the other way. Because errors are squared, one far-away point can dominate the loss, so aim for the middle of the whole cloud rather than the points nearest your line.
level.w1-l3.notes.idea: Picture the loss as a landscape. Every spot on the map is one choice of the model's two parameters, and its height is the loss there, so training means finding the lowest point. Gradient descent gets there by feeling the slope where it stands and stepping downhill, again and again.
level.w1-l3.notes.controls: Choose a step size, then press Take a step: the ball moves along the downhill arrow by that amount. The hollow ball shows where the step will land before you commit. You have a limited number of steps.
level.w1-l3.notes.reading: The rings are contour lines: each one joins places with the same loss, like height lines on a hiking map. Rings packed close together mean steep ground, and rings far apart mean flat ground. On steep ground a big step overshoots; on flat ground a small step barely moves.
level.w1-l4.notes.idea: Now gradient descent runs on its own, one step per epoch, and the learning rate is the size of every step. Too small, and the model creeps toward the answer and runs out of time. Too large, and it overshoots the valley, bouncing from side to side or flying off entirely: the loss blows up.
level.w1-l4.notes.controls: Pick a learning rate with the slider and press Train. The run replays epoch by epoch: the line moves on the data and the loss curve draws beside it. You can train as often as you like.
level.w1-l4.notes.reading: The loss curve shows the loss after each epoch on a logarithmic scale, so each step down the chart is a big improvement. A smooth, slow slope means the rate is too small. A zigzag, or a curve that climbs, means it is too large. You want the curve to flatten out (converge) within the epoch limit.
level.w1-l5.notes.idea: Real loss landscapes can have several valleys. Gradient descent only feels the slope right under it, so it settles in whichever valley it starts above and cannot climb out. The deepest valley is the global minimum; a valley that is only the lowest nearby is a local minimum.
level.w1-l5.notes.controls: Click or tap the map to place the ball, or focus the map and move it with the arrow keys. Then press Roll the ball and gradient descent carries it downhill by itself. Where it starts is your only decision.
level.w1-l5.notes.reading: Read the contour rings like a hiking map: more rings nested inside each other means a deeper valley. The ridges between valleys decide which way the ball rolls, so check which side of a ridge your starting point is on.
level.w1-l6.notes.idea: Some measurements are simply wrong: a broken sensor, a typo. These outliers sit far from the pattern of the rest. Because the loss squares errors, one outlier far away pulls the best-fit line toward itself and spoils the fit for everyone else.
level.w1-l6.notes.controls: The line is always the best fit through the points you keep. Click or tap a point to remove it, and again to put it back (keyboard: Tab to a point, then press Enter). Put all points back starts over. When you're done, Check against new data tests the line on measurements it has never seen.
level.w1-l6.notes.reading: The long vertical error lines point at suspects. Watch the line as you remove a point: taking out an outlier makes it swing back toward the trend, while taking out a normal point barely moves it. Real data is precious, so removing good points counts against you.
level.w1-l7.notes.idea: This model has two inputs, and one is about ten times bigger than the other. Big inputs stretch the loss landscape into a long, narrow valley, where any step size that is safe across the narrow side is painfully slow along the long side. Scaling puts every feature on a similar range, so the valley becomes round and big steps become safe.
level.w1-l7.notes.controls: Scale the features switches standardization on or off: subtract each feature's mean, then divide by its spread. The learning rate slider and Train work as in Too Fast, Too Slow. The goal is to converge at least 3 times faster than the best run without scaling.
level.w1-l7.notes.reading: Feature ranges shows each input's raw values next to its values after scaling. The loss chart draws the best unscaled run next to yours, so compare how many epochs each one needs to converge.
level.w1-l8.notes.idea: Real data usually needs preparing before training works at all. This level has World 1's problems at once: a few broken points dragging the line away from the trend, an input on a large scale that makes the loss valley narrow, and a tight epoch budget. Prepare the data first, then train.
level.w1-l8.notes.controls: Click or tap points to remove them before training, and again to put them back. Scale the feature standardizes x. Then pick a learning rate and press Train. The line is judged on fresh data.
level.w1-l8.notes.reading: If training blows up at every learning rate, the scale is the problem. If it converges but misses the fresh data, look for points far from the trend. The loss curve shows how fast training converged against the epoch budget.
level.w2-l1.notes.idea: Not every prediction is a number. Classification predicts a category: which kingdom does this person belong to? A linear classifier draws one straight line, the decision boundary, and labels everyone by the side they fall on.
level.w2-l1.notes.controls: Drag the two orange handles to place the border, or focus a handle and use the arrow keys (hold Shift for bigger moves). Swap sides flips which kingdom gets which side. Press Check the border to be judged.
level.w2-l1.notes.reading: The shading shows which kingdom each side belongs to, so circles and squares on the wrong shade are mistakes. The count under the controls says how many people are on their own kingdom's side. Accuracy is that count divided by everyone.
level.w2-l2.notes.idea: A good classifier doesn't just pick a side; it says how sure it is. Logistic regression turns a score into a probability with the sigmoid curve: close to 0% on one side, close to 100% on the other, and exactly 50/50 at the threshold. Confidence has to be earned, because being sure and wrong costs far more than being unsure.
level.w2-l2.notes.controls: Threshold moves the point where the model is exactly 50/50. Slope sets how quickly it switches from square to circle: steeper means more certain. Press Check the confidence when you're ready.
level.w2-l2.notes.reading: The curve shows the probability of circle, from 0 at the bottom to 1 at the top. Squares belong low and circles high, and the dashed lines mark 80% confidence on each side. The readout names your least confident point. Points the model hasn't seen are judged too, so a curve that is too steep can be confidently wrong near the border.
level.w2-l3.notes.idea: A linear model can only draw a straight border in the features it is given, but you choose the features. Give it new ones made from the raw inputs, like x₁² or x₁·x₂, and a straight border in those features becomes a curve on the map. The right features are often worth more than a fancier model.
level.w2-l3.notes.controls: Tick the features the model sees: x₁, x₂, their squares and their product. Press Train to fit the model and see its border. Fewer, well-chosen features beat including everything.
level.w2-l3.notes.reading: The shaded regions show which kingdom the trained model assigns to every spot on the map, and the edge between them is its border. The readout says how many training points it gets right, and with which features.
level.w2-l4.notes.idea: Scoring well on the data you trained on is easy: a flexible enough model can memorize it, noise and all. What matters is how it does on people it has never seen. A model that fits the training data better than the real pattern is overfitting, and it happens most with little data and lots of flexibility.
level.w2-l4.notes.controls: Complexity sets the polynomial degree: 1 is a straight border, and each step up gives the model more inputs so its border can bend more. Train shows the border and the training score only. Check on new people judges the model on people it hasn't seen.
level.w2-l4.notes.reading: After a check, the new people appear as hollow marks and the ones on the wrong side are crossed out. A border that loops around single training points is a warning sign, even when the training score is 100%.
level.w2-l5.notes.idea: Sometimes you want a flexible model without its bad habits. Regularization adds a penalty for large weights to the loss, so the model can only bend its border where the data really demands it. The border comes out smoother: a little worse on the training data, better on new data.
level.w2-l5.notes.controls: The degree is fixed high here, so the model has 27 inputs. Regularization strength (λ) sets the penalty: 0 means none, and higher values force a smoother border. Train shows the border and the training score. Check on new people compares the two scores.
level.w2-l5.notes.reading: Compare accuracy on the training people with accuracy on new people. If training is far ahead, the model is memorizing: turn λ up. If training drops below new people, the penalty is so strong the model can't fit what it has seen: turn λ down. You want the two to meet.
level.w2-l6.notes.idea: When one group is rare, a model can look good by mostly ignoring it. If 9 in 10 people are lowlanders, calling everyone a lowlander is 90% accurate and finds nobody. Recall asks the better question for the rare group: of the hill folk that exist, how many did the model find?
level.w2-l6.notes.controls: Weight of each hill-clan point makes every hill-clan training point count as several people, so missing one costs the model more (this is called oversampling). Train shows the border and what it finds. Check on new people measures recall on people it hasn't seen.
level.w2-l6.notes.reading: The training line counts hill folk found and lowlanders right separately, which one accuracy number would hide. Heavier hill-clan points are drawn bigger. Too little weight misses the hill folk, and too much starts calling lowlanders hill folk, so watch both counts.
level.w2-l7.notes.idea: The model gives everyone a probability of being hill folk, and the threshold decides how sure it must be before it acts. Lower the threshold and it finds more of the people you want (recall goes up), but it also picks more of the wrong ones (precision goes down). There's no free lunch, only a choice of balance.
level.w2-l7.notes.controls: The model is already trained. Your only control is the threshold: invite when the model is at least this sure. Moving it shifts the border and updates the matrix at once, without retraining. Check on new people judges the result.
level.w2-l7.notes.reading: The confusion matrix counts the training people four ways: rows are who they really are, columns are what the model decided. Found and rightly left out are correct; missed and invited by mistake are errors. Recall = found ÷ all hill folk. Precision = found ÷ everyone invited.
level.w2-l8.notes.idea: F1 combines precision and recall into one score, their harmonic mean. It's only high when both are high, so it can't be gamed by flagging everyone (precision collapses) or no one (recall is 0). This level uses the whole toolkit: a curve for the shape, restraint against the noise, and a fair say for the rare raiders.
level.w2-l8.notes.controls: Complexity bends the border, regularization (λ) smooths it, and the weight of each raider point rebalances training: press Train after changing any of them. The threshold then moves the border of the trained model without retraining, and the matrix updates as you move it.
level.w2-l8.notes.reading: Under the matrix you'll find recall, precision and F1 for the training people. Training scores flatter a flexible model, so if the border twists around single points, expect worse on new people. After Check on new people, the crossed-out marks show exactly where the border fails.
level.w3-l1.mission: Safe mushrooms are green circles, poisonous ones ochre squares. Ask one yes/no question that sorts them, then check it on new mushrooms.
level.w3-l1.hint1: Try a question about stem height, then one about cap width. Which one actually separates the two kinds?
level.w3-l1.hint2: Only cap width matters here. Move the cut until each side is as pure as you can make it: watch the training count.
level.w3-l1.hint3: Cut cap width at about 6.2 cm.
level.w3-l1.debrief: That was a decision tree with a single question, often called a decision stump. A tree sorts by asking yes/no questions about one measurement at a time, and every region predicts the kind most common in it.
level.w3-l1.notes.idea: A decision tree predicts by asking yes/no questions, one measurement at a time: “Is the cap narrower than 6 cm?” Each question cuts the map in two with a straight line along one axis, and each side predicts the kind of mushroom most common in it.
level.w3-l1.notes.controls: The dashed outline marks the region your question will cut. Choose Split by cap width (a vertical cut) or Split by stem height (a horizontal cut). Then drag the orange line, or focus it and use the arrow keys, to move it. Remove the last question to start again.
level.w3-l1.notes.reading: Each side is shaded by what it predicts: green for safe, ochre for poisonous. The tree below the map spells out the question and how many mushrooms of each kind landed on each side. After a check, the new mushrooms appear as hollow marks, crossed out where the tree got them wrong.
level.w3-l2.mission: Poisonous mushrooms hide in one corner. One cut can't fence them in. Ask a second question inside the right region, then check.
level.w3-l2.hint1: Ask your best single question first and look at the tree: one of its two groups is still mixed.
level.w3-l2.hint2: Click that mixed region on the map to select it, then ask a question about the other measurement inside it.
level.w3-l2.hint3: Split cap width at 3.8 cm, then split the left region by stem height at 5.1 cm.
level.w3-l2.debrief: That was a deeper tree. Each question splits one region again, so a tree of depth two can fence in a corner that no single straight cut can. The more levels, the more complicated the shapes a tree can draw.
level.w3-l2.notes.idea: A tree doesn't have to ask the same question everywhere. After the first cut, each side can ask its own next question. That's how trees carve out corners and blocks: each extra level of questions splits one region into two smaller ones.
level.w3-l2.notes.controls: Click a region on the map (or Tab to it and press Enter) to select it: the dashed outline shows where your next question goes. Then choose Split by cap width or Split by stem height, and drag the new cut into place. You have up to three questions.
level.w3-l2.notes.reading: The tree below the map grows with every question: follow Yes and No down to each final group and read how many safe and poisonous mushrooms ended up there. A group with both kinds is still mixed and needs another question. The best trees here ask as few questions as they need.
level.w3-l3.mission: Sort the mushrooms into baskets that are as pure as you can make them. Watch each basket's impurity, then check on new mushrooms.
level.w3-l3.hint1: Start with the cut that makes one side almost entirely one kind: the impurity readout drops the most there.
level.w3-l3.hint2: A question can lower impurity even when the training count doesn't change. Trust the impurity: it's setting up the next question.
level.w3-l3.hint3: Cap width at 7.1 cm, then cap width at 2.9 cm on the left, then stem height at 4.3 cm on the far left. Nudge each cut until the impurity is lowest.
level.w3-l3.debrief: That was Gini impurity, the measure real decision trees use to choose their questions. A tree tries every possible cut and keeps the one that makes its groups purest. You saw why: a question can make the groups purer before it changes a single prediction, and that sets up the next one.
level.w3-l3.notes.idea: How does a tree pick its questions? It measures how mixed each group is. Gini impurity is 0 when a group is all one kind and 0.5 when it's an even mix. The tree tries every possible cut and keeps the one that lowers the average impurity of its groups the most.
level.w3-l3.notes.controls: As before: select a region, choose Split by cap width or Split by stem height, and drag the cut (or use the arrow keys, Shift for bigger steps). You have three questions. The impurity updates with every move, so you can tune a cut until the number is lowest.
level.w3-l3.notes.reading: Under the controls, Tree impurity is the weighted average over all final groups: lower is purer. In the tree below the map, each group shows its own Gini. Watch for a question that lowers impurity while the training count stays the same: it hasn't changed any prediction yet, but it has separated the kinds a little, ready for the next question.
level.w3-l4.mission: Now the machine grows the tree. It only saw 70 mushrooms, and some are mislabelled. Limit its depth, then check it on new mushrooms: sort at least 80% right.
level.w3-l4.hint1: Train at full depth and look at the boxes: some surround a single mushroom. Is that a real pattern or a mistake in the labels?
level.w3-l4.hint2: A 100% training score is the warning sign here. Try the shallowest trees too: too few questions can't see the pattern either.
level.w3-l4.hint3: A depth of 3 fits the real pattern.
level.w3-l4.debrief: That was overfitting, tree style. A deep tree keeps asking questions until every training mushroom sits in its own pure box, mislabelled ones included, so it scores 100% and sorts new mushrooms worse. Too shallow and it can't see the pattern at all. The right depth sits in between.
level.w3-l4.notes.idea: A real tree-growing algorithm keeps splitting while it can make its groups purer. With no limit, it only stops when every group is pure, even if that means a tiny box around one mislabelled mushroom. Limiting the depth, the number of questions in a row, stops it from chasing single points.
level.w3-l4.notes.controls: Maximum depth sets how many questions in a row the tree may ask. Train grows the tree and shows its boxes and training score. Check on new mushrooms judges it on mushrooms it has never seen.
level.w3-l4.notes.reading: The boxes on the map are the tree's leaves, shaded by what they predict. Many tiny boxes around single mushrooms mean memorizing. Under the controls, the tree's size is its number of leaves and how many questions deep it goes. After a check, crossed-out hollow marks show the new mushrooms it got wrong.
level.w3-l5.mission: This tree may grow ten questions deep. Instead of cutting its depth, forbid tiny leaves: make the train and new-mushroom scores agree within 5 points, with at least 80% of new ones right.
level.w3-l5.hint1: Train with 1 mushroom per leaf and count the boxes: the tree gives stray mushrooms boxes of their own.
level.w3-l5.hint2: Raise the minimum and watch the leaf count fall while the score on new mushrooms holds. Go too far and the tree becomes too crude.
level.w3-l5.hint3: Somewhere between 5 and 15 mushrooms per leaf works; nearer 15 gives the smallest tree.
level.w3-l5.debrief: That was pruning. Requiring a minimum number of mushrooms per leaf removes the branches that only fit noise, so the tree shrinks from 18 leaves to a handful without losing accuracy on new mushrooms. Prune too hard and it can't fit the real pattern either.
level.w3-l5.notes.idea: Depth isn't the only way to stop a tree from memorizing. You can also forbid small leaves: a question is only allowed if both sides keep enough mushrooms. Branches that exist only to fence in one or two stray points can't form, a bit like pruning the thin twigs off a real tree.
level.w3-l5.notes.controls: Minimum mushrooms per leaf sets the smallest group a leaf may hold. The depth limit is fixed at 10 here. Train grows the tree; Check on new mushrooms compares its training and new-mushroom scores.
level.w3-l5.notes.reading: Watch the number of leaves under the controls as you raise the minimum: the tree gets simpler. Compare the two scores after a check: a big gap with training ahead means it still memorizes. If both scores drop together, you pruned too hard. The best trees here are small and agree with themselves.
level.w3-l6.mission: The forest's tree is regrown every season from a fresh handful of mushrooms. Foragers need its advice not to flip each time. Pick a depth whose retrained trees agree, and still sort 75% of new mushrooms right.
level.w3-l6.hint1: Train at full depth and look at the faint orange lines: each is a tree regrown from a resampled handful of mushrooms. Do they agree?
level.w3-l6.hint2: Deep trees follow whichever mushrooms they happened to see, so their borders scatter. One question is steady but crude. Look for the depth in between.
level.w3-l6.hint3: Three questions deep is both steady and accurate.
level.w3-l6.debrief: That was the bias-variance trade-off. A one-question tree is steady but crude: high bias. A deep tree fits whatever sample it gets, so retrained versions disagree: high variance, even when today's score looks fine. Good models keep both low; next, you'll see how a forest gets depth without the wobble.
level.w3-l6.notes.idea: A model is only as trustworthy as it is repeatable. If a slightly different sample of mushrooms gives a very different tree, its advice is partly luck: that's variance. A model too simple to change is steady but misses the real pattern: that's bias. The best depth keeps both small.
level.w3-l6.notes.controls: Maximum depth sets how many questions in a row the tree may ask. Train grows the tree from all your mushrooms, plus 8 more trees from resampled handfuls (mushrooms drawn at random, with repeats), shown as faint orange lines. Check judges on new mushrooms.
level.w3-l6.notes.reading: The shaded boxes are your tree. The faint orange lines are the borders of the 8 retrained trees: tight together means steady, scattered means shaky. Under the controls, the disagreement shows how much of the map those trees can't agree on. You need 8% or less, and at least 75% of new mushrooms right; 80% or more earns more stars.
level.w3-l7.mission: One deep tree wobbles with every handful of mushrooms. Plant a forest: many deep trees, each grown on its own resampled handful, voting together. Sort at least 78% of new mushrooms right.
level.w3-l7.hint1: Train with one tree and look at its border: jagged, and it chases single mushrooms. Then try a handful of trees.
level.w3-l7.hint2: Each tree overfits in its own direction. Averaging many of them cancels those errors out: more trees, smoother border.
level.w3-l7.hint3: Around 20 to 30 trees is plenty here.
level.w3-l7.debrief: That was bagging (bootstrap aggregating). Every tree is deep and overfits, but each overfits its own resampled handful, so their mistakes point in different directions. Averaging their votes cancels much of the wobble: the forest sorts new mushrooms far better than any one of its trees.
level.w3-l7.notes.idea: You saw that deep trees are shaky: each one depends on the sample it got. Bagging turns that into a strength. Grow many deep trees, each on its own random resample of the data, and let them vote. Their individual mistakes differ, so the average is steadier and more accurate than any single tree.
level.w3-l7.notes.controls: Number of trees sets how many deep trees vote. Each grows on a bootstrap sample: the same number of mushrooms drawn at random, with repeats. Train grows the forest and shows its combined border; Check on new mushrooms judges the vote.
level.w3-l7.notes.reading: The shading and orange border show the forest's majority vote. With one tree the border is jagged and hugs single mushrooms; as you add trees it smooths into the real divide. The training score stays high either way: every deep tree fits its sample, so only the check on new mushrooms shows the gain.
level.w3-l8.mission: Deep in the old forest, safe mushrooms grow in a ring and the records are noisy. Grow a forest that sorts new mushrooms well: at least 76.5% right. Every tool from this world is yours.
level.w3-l8.hint1: Check what one deep tree does, then what the best single tree can do. Neither is enough here: you'll need many trees voting.
level.w3-l8.hint2: More trees alone won't do it: each deep tree still chases the noise. Limit the trees too, by depth or by leaf size, and let many of them vote.
level.w3-l8.hint3: Try 30 trees, a depth of 4 and at least 3 mushrooms per leaf.
level.w3-l8.debrief: That was a random forest: many limited trees, each grown on its own resampled handful, voting together. Limits keep each tree from memorizing the noise, and the vote cancels what wobble is left. Full random forests also let each question consider only a random subset of the measurements, which makes trees more different; with just two measurements here, that trick adds little, so resampling and good limits did the work. You've tamed the Forest of Trees.
level.w3-l8.notes.idea: Everything from this world at once: a tree can overfit by growing too deep or keeping tiny leaves (levels 4 and 5), deep trees are shaky (level 6), and many trees voting cancel that shakiness (level 7). A random forest combines them: limit each tree, grow many on resampled data, and let them vote.
level.w3-l8.notes.controls: Maximum depth and Minimum mushrooms per leaf limit each tree; Number of trees sets how many vote. Train grows the forest and shows its combined border and training score; Check on new mushrooms judges it.
level.w3-l8.notes.reading: The shading and orange border are the forest's vote. The training score says little here: deep trees reach 100% on what they saw. Compare checks instead, and look at the border: a smooth ring means the forest found the pattern, a ragged one means it's still following the noise.
